passage:
Fresh out of the bath in their Pune flat, Jagdish wriggled free of the towel and ran down the corridor, giggling. At the bedroom door he stopped and looked back over his shoulder, grinning at Hemant.
"I'm coming to get you!" Hemant said, taking big slow steps.
Jagdish shrieked, ran behind the curtain, and peeped out again, waiting.

qa.q: Where did Jagdish hide?
qa.a: Behind the curtain.

qa.q: What did Jagdish's look back over his shoulder mean?
qa.a: It was an invitation to play; he felt playful and excited and wanted Hemant to chase him.

qa.q: What did Hemant do that built connection?
qa.a: He accepted the invitation and chased with big slow steps, keeping the game fun and safe.

qa.q: What would change if Hemant had just scolded him to come back and dress?
qa.a: Jagdish would miss the playful connection, and getting dressed might have turned into a struggle.

grounding: A toddler runs off grinning and looks back to be chased, and his father joins the game.

passage:
"She's running away from me again!" said Dadi, puffing.
Sabina stopped at the end of the hall and looked back, grinning.
"Look, she's waiting," said Kalyani, her mother. "She wants you to chase her."
"Oh! I'm coming, I'm coming!"
Sabina squealed and ran. At the wall she turned round, and this time ran at Dadi.
"Now you're chasing me?" Dadi laughed, and turned to run.

qa.q: Who chased Sabina?
qa.a: Dadi.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she looked back grinning?
qa.a: She was playful and happy, inviting Dadi to chase her.

qa.q: How did Kalyani help Dadi understand Sabina?
qa.a: She pointed out that Sabina's look back meant she wanted to be chased, not that she was running away.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel when Sabina turns to chase her?
qa.a: Dadi likely feels delighted and amused, enjoying the turn-taking game.

grounding: A mother helps a grandmother see that a toddler's grinning look back is an invitation to chase, building turn-taking.

passage: Childminder's note, Tuesday. In the garden, Rashmi ran off toward the hedge, then stopped and looked back at me with a huge grin. I took the hint and chased her, slowly, saying "I'm going to catch you!" She shrieked. After a few rounds, she stopped, turned round and ran after me instead. We took turns until snack time. She is starting to understand the game goes both ways. Nirmala, childminder

qa.q: What did Rashmi do after a few rounds?
qa.a: She stopped, turned round and ran after Nirmala instead.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she looked back with a grin?
qa.a: She felt playful and excited, and was inviting Nirmala to chase her.

qa.q: What did Nirmala's joining in help Rashmi learn?
qa.a: Turn-taking, since the chasing game went both ways.

qa.q: How might Rashmi's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They would likely feel happy to hear she had such fun and is learning to take turns.

grounding: A childminder joins a toddler's look-back chasing game, and they take turns.

passage:
The shopping centre in Chennai was packed and noisy, music blaring from every shop. Uma started screaming in her stroller and arched her back, pushing away.
"Stop it, Uma! Everyone's looking," said Suraj, her father.
She screamed louder, and the arching got worse.
Suraj stopped, unbuckled her and held her close. He carried her to a quiet stairwell. There, pressed against his chest, she slowly stopped shaking.

qa.q: Where did Suraj carry Uma?
qa.a: To a quiet stairwell.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she screamed and arched?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed and frightened by the crowd and loud music.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Scolding made her more upset; holding her close and moving somewhere quiet calmed her.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel about the next trip to the shopping centre?
qa.a: He might feel wary and plan to avoid the busiest times, now that he knows what upset her.

grounding: A father learns that scolding his distressed toddler makes things worse and calm closeness in a quiet place helps.

passage:
"Hold him tight, sir," said the barber, lifting the buzzing clippers.
Gautam screamed and arched away, clawing at his father.
"He's just being dramatic. Keep him still," said the man waiting next.
"No." Nitin turned the chair away. "Stop, please. He's terrified."
The barber switched the clippers off. Nitin held Gautam close until his breathing slowed.
"Scissors today, sitting on my lap?" Nitin asked the barber. "And quietly."

qa.q: What did the barber switch off?
qa.a: The buzzing clippers.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he screamed and arched away?
qa.a: He was terrified of the buzzing clippers and overwhelmed.

qa.q: Which of Nitin's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Stopping, holding Gautam close and changing to scissors on his lap helped, because it calmed him and removed the trigger.

qa.q: How does the man waiting next see Gautam's screaming?
qa.a: He thinks Gautam is being dramatic, not frightened.

grounding: A father stops a haircut when his toddler is terrified, offering closeness and removing the trigger.

passage: Daycare note, Friday. During today's fire alarm test, Avni screamed and clung to me. When another staff member tried to take her so I could help the others, she arched away, screaming harder. I kept her, held her close and took her into the quiet room until she calmed. For the next test we will warn her first, hold her before it starts and cover her ears. Maria, daycare teacher

qa.q: What happened today at daycare?
qa.a: A fire alarm test.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she arched away from the other staff member?
qa.a: She was frightened and overwhelmed, and needed the person she was already clinging to.

qa.q: What is the plan for the next alarm test?
qa.a: To warn her first, hold her before it starts and cover her ears.

qa.q: How might Avni's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They might feel worried about her fright but reassured by the calm care and the plan.

grounding: A teacher calms a distressed toddler with closeness during an alarm test and plans to prevent it next time.

passage:
In their Delhi flat, Uday suddenly refused to walk after playing on the sofa. He sat still, holding his left arm against his tummy. When Anjali tried to lift him under the arms, he let out a sharp cry.
She didn't call it a tantrum. She noticed he wouldn't use the arm at all, not even to take his biscuit. She rang the doctor, and they went that same afternoon.

qa.q: Which arm did Uday hold against his tummy?
qa.a: His left arm.

qa.q: What was Uday likely feeling when he held his arm and cried sharply?
qa.a: He was in pain, and frightened of being moved.

qa.q: What did Anjali notice that made her act?
qa.a: That he guarded the arm and wouldn't use it even for a biscuit, so she took him to the doctor that afternoon.

qa.q: What would change if Anjali had seen it as a tantrum?
qa.a: Uday's pain might have gone unchecked, and he would have suffered longer.

grounding: A mother watches for guarding and refusal to move rather than calling it a tantrum, and gets her hurt toddler checked.

passage:
"She's not eating again," said Madhuri. "Just pushes the plate."
"She's fussy," said Lalremsiami's father.
"Look at her. She keeps pointing at her mouth. And there's so much drool."
Lalremsiami whimpered and pushed a finger into her cheek.
"Her back tooth?" He looked. "Red and swollen. Poor thing."
"Something cold to chew, then. And if it keeps going or worries us, we see the doctor."

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami keep pointing at?
qa.a: Her mouth.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she whimpered and pushed her cheek?
qa.a: She was in pain and uncomfortable, probably from a new back tooth.

qa.q: What did Madhuri notice that her husband missed?
qa.a: That Lalremsiami was pointing at her mouth and drooling, signs of pain rather than fussiness.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami's father see things by the end?
qa.a: He moves from calling her fussy to feeling sorry for her once he sees the swollen gum.

grounding: Parents read a toddler's pointing, drooling and refusal of food as pain rather than fussiness.

passage: Daycare note, Wednesday. Jagdish fell off the low step in the garden this morning. He cried sharply and then sat holding his right ankle, refusing to stand. I did not ask him to walk. I kept him still, put a cold pack on, and rang his parents straight away. His mother collected him before lunch and took him to the doctor that afternoon. Pooja, daycare teacher

qa.q: Which ankle did Jagdish hold?
qa.a: His right ankle.

qa.q: What was Jagdish likely feeling when he refused to stand?
qa.a: He was in pain and afraid to put weight on his ankle.

qa.q: Which choices of Pooja's were wise, and why?
qa.a: Not making him walk, keeping him still with a cold pack and calling his parents straight away were wise, because a toddler can't say how bad it is.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's mother feel when she gets the call?
qa.a: She would likely feel worried, and grateful to be told quickly.

grounding: A teacher reads a toddler's sharp cry and refusal to stand as pain and gets him checked the same day.

passage:
In their Copenhagen flat, Zanele's wooden boat cracked in half when it fell off the table. She didn't cry. She went very quiet, lay down on the rug with the two pieces, and stared at them, drooping.
"Tired already?" asked Emil, her father. Then he looked closer. "Oh. Your boat broke. You're sad."
Zanele's lip wobbled, and she let him lift her into his lap.

qa.q: What broke?
qa.a: Zanele's wooden boat.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling when she lay quietly with the pieces?
qa.a: She was sad about her broken boat, even though at first it looked like tiredness.

qa.q: What did Emil do that helped?
qa.a: He looked closer, named her sadness and offered comfort in his lap.

qa.q: What would change if Emil had put her to bed thinking she was tired?
qa.a: Her sadness would go unnoticed, and she wouldn't get the comfort or the word for her feeling.

grounding: A father notices his toddler's quiet drooping is sadness at a broken toy, not tiredness, and names it.

passage: I'm Gautam, Sumit's cousin. After Dadi left for the station on Sunday, Sumit sat on the steps very quietly with his head down, pulling at a thread on his shorts. He didn't want to play. I thought he was sleepy. But his mother sat beside him and said, "You miss Dadi, don't you?" He climbed into her lap and whimpered. I think she was right. He wasn't sleepy. He was sad.

qa.q: Who left for the station?
qa.a: Dadi.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling as he sat with his head down?
qa.a: He was sad and missing Dadi, though it looked like sleepiness.

qa.q: What did Sumit's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She named his feeling, "You miss Dadi", and offered comfort.

qa.q: How does Gautam see Sumit's quietness by the end?
qa.a: Gautam realises Sumit was sad, not sleepy.

grounding: A cousin learns that a toddler's quiet drooping after his grandmother leaves is sadness, as his mother names it.

passage:
Monday: Dilnaz's Abbu left for a week's work trip. She stood at the door, whimpering.
Wednesday: she was very quiet and droopy, pushing her blocks away. Keerthana, her nanny, thought she was tired, then remembered. "You miss Abbu. That's sad." Dilnaz leaned into her.
The next Monday: the door opened, and there was Abbu. Dilnaz shrieked and ran to him.

qa.q: What kind of trip did Abbu leave for?
qa.a: A week's work trip.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling on Wednesday when she pushed her blocks away?
qa.a: She was sad and missing her Abbu, which looked like tiredness at first.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do that helped on Wednesday?
qa.a: She named the feeling, "You miss Abbu", and let Dilnaz lean on her for comfort.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel when Dilnaz shrieks and runs to him?
qa.a: He would likely feel joyful and relieved to be home. 🤍

grounding: Over a week a nanny recognises a toddler's quiet drooping as sadness at a parent's absence and names it.

passage:
At the Saturday market in Rome, Nadia burst into loud tears, her cheeks wet. Sofia, her mother, crouched and picked her up first. "Shh, I've got you."
Then she checked. Nadia had eaten. It wasn't nap time. Nadia kicked her foot and cried harder. Sofia took off the sandal. A little stone fell out. Nadia sniffed, and the tears slowed.

qa.q: What fell out of Nadia's sandal?
qa.a: A little stone.

qa.q: What was Nadia feeling when she cried and kicked her foot?
qa.a: She was hurting and frustrated from the stone in her sandal.

qa.q: Which order of Sofia's steps helped, and why?
qa.a: Soothing first, then checking hunger, sleep and her foot helped, because Nadia calmed while Sofia found the real cause.

qa.q: What would change if Sofia had told her to stop crying and walk on?
qa.a: The stone would have stayed, and Nadia would have kept crying and hurting.

grounding: A mother soothes her crying toddler first, then checks her needs until she finds a stone in her sandal.

passage: I'm Avni, Trisha's big sister. On Friday the neighbours' dog barked right behind the gate, and Trisha burst into tears, loud ones, with her face all wet. I started to explain, "It's behind the gate, silly." Mummy didn't explain. She scooped Trisha up and rocked her until the crying stopped. Only then did she say, "The dog is behind the gate. It can't come out." Trisha looked, sniffing. It worked better her way.

qa.q: Where was the dog?
qa.a: Right behind the gate.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when she burst into tears?
qa.a: She was frightened by the sudden barking.

qa.q: Why did Mummy's way work better than Avni's?
qa.a: She soothed Trisha first and explained only when she was calm, so Trisha could take it in.

qa.q: How does Avni see the moment afterwards?
qa.a: Avni realises that soothing before explaining worked better than her own explanation.

grounding: A sister sees their mother soothe a crying toddler first and explain later, which works better than reasoning.

passage:
Monday before lunch: Aadhya cried loudly, tears everywhere. Himani explained, "Lunch in five minutes, sweetie." The crying went on until the food came.
Wednesday: the same hungry cry. Himani picked her up first, held her, then gave her a banana. Aadhya calmed quickly.
Saturday night: tearful and rubbing her eyes. Himani cuddled her and hummed. She fell asleep.

qa.q: What did Himani give Aadhya on Wednesday?
qa.a: A banana.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling behind the tears on Saturday night?
qa.a: She was tired, rubbing her eyes and needing comfort to fall asleep.

qa.q: What did Himani learn over the week?
qa.a: To soothe and meet the need first, since explaining to a crying toddler doesn't help.

qa.q: How might Himani feel on Saturday night?
qa.a: She would likely feel calm and more confident in reading Aadhya's tears.

grounding: Over a week a mother learns to soothe and meet her toddler's needs before reasoning with her tears.

passage:
Papa was leaving on the scooter for the market, and Preeti wanted to go. When Parul, her mother, said no, Preeti stamped her feet in the dust of the courtyard and threw her steel tumbler. It clanged against the wall.
Parul knelt and held her hands. "You're angry. You wanted to go with Papa. No throwing." Preeti stamped once more, crying. Parul held her until the scooter was gone, and then Preeti waved after it.

qa.q: What did Preeti throw?
qa.a: Her steel tumbler.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she stamped and threw the tumbler?
qa.a: She was angry and frustrated at not being allowed to go with Papa.

qa.q: What did Parul do that helped more than punishment would?
qa.a: She named the anger, set a calm limit about throwing and held Preeti until she calmed.

qa.q: How might Papa feel seeing Preeti wave after him?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved that she calmed down and touched that she still waved.

grounding: A mother answers her toddler's stamping and throwing with calm limits and a name for her anger.

passage:
At the kitchen table in their Berlin flat, Emeka tried to jam a puzzle piece into the wrong hole. It wouldn't go. He banged his fist on the table and shouted, then hit the puzzle board.
Zeynep, his babysitter, held his hand gently. "Angry! It won't go. No hitting. You can stamp your feet."
Emeka stamped, hard, three times. Then he looked at the piece again, turned it and pushed it in.

qa.q: What was Emeka trying to fit?
qa.a: A puzzle piece.

qa.q: What was Emeka feeling when he banged the table?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated that the piece wouldn't fit.

qa.q: What made Zeynep's response work?
qa.a: She stayed calm, named the anger, stopped the hitting and offered a safe action, stamping.

qa.q: What would change if Zeynep had punished him?
qa.a: Emeka might have become more upset and given up on the puzzle.

grounding: A babysitter answers a toddler's angry hitting with calm limits, a named feeling and a safe outlet.

passage: I'm Arohi. I live next door to little Sharmila. On Thursday, when it was time for her to leave our house, she threw both her sandals at the car, one after the other, stamping and shouting. I half expected a smack. Her mother just picked up the sandals and said calmly, "You're angry. You didn't want to go. Sandals are for feet." Sharmila stamped once more, then let her mother buckle them on.

qa.q: What did Sharmila throw?
qa.a: Both her sandals, at the car.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have been feeling when she threw her sandals?
qa.a: She was probably angry and frustrated at having to leave.

qa.q: What did the mother's calm response do?
qa.a: It named the feeling, set a limit and helped Sharmila settle without making the anger bigger.

qa.q: How does Arohi see the mother's reaction?
qa.a: Arohi is surprised, having expected a smack, and notices how calm she was.

grounding: A neighbour sees a mother answer her toddler's angry throwing with calm and a named feeling, not punishment.

passage:
Every evening, Pranav took the buffalo to the pond, and every evening little Zubin clung to their mother's leg and cried when it came near.
"Don't be a baby, touch it!" Pranav said on Tuesday.
"No forcing," said their mother. She sat with Zubin on the step, far off, and they just watched the buffalo drink.
By the end of the week, Zubin stood at the edge of the yard, holding her hand, watching it go by.

qa.q: Where did Pranav take the buffalo every evening?
qa.a: To the pond.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he clung and cried?
qa.a: He was frightened of the big buffalo.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, and why?
qa.a: Watching from a distance with his mother, a little closer each day, worked better than being forced, because Zubin felt safe.

qa.q: How does Pranav see Zubin's fear at first?
qa.a: Pranav sees it as babyish and wants him to be brave by touching it.

grounding: A mother uses comfort and gradual distance rather than forcing her toddler to face his fear of a buffalo.

passage:
The vacuum cleaner roared on in their Toronto living room. Esther froze, then ran and clung to Gabriel's leg, crying.
Gabriel switched it off. "Loud, huh? It's off now."
He sat on the floor with her beside the silent vacuum. She watched it for a long time, then touched it with one finger. "Ready for a short noise?" he asked, holding her close. He switched it on for a second, then off. She flinched, but didn't cry.

qa.q: What did Esther touch with one finger?
qa.a: The silent vacuum cleaner.

qa.q: What was Esther feeling when she froze and clung to Gabriel?
qa.a: She was frightened by the loud roar of the vacuum.

qa.q: What did Gabriel do that helped Esther's fear?
qa.a: He comforted her, let her explore the switched-off vacuum and then tried a short noise while holding her.

qa.q: What would change if Gabriel had laughed and kept vacuuming?
qa.a: Esther would likely have felt more scared and stayed afraid of it.

grounding: A father comforts his fearful toddler and exposes her gradually to the vacuum rather than forcing or mocking.

passage: I'm Lalit, and I was chatting with Zeenat's mother in the lane when the neighbour's big dog trotted up. Zeenat froze, then clung to her mother's legs and cried. A boy nearby laughed. "Scaredy!" Her mother didn't laugh. She picked Zeenat up and stepped back, far from the dog. "It's a big dog. You're safe." They stood and watched it from there. I wondered if Zeenat would ever like dogs.

qa.q: What did the boy nearby say?
qa.a: "Scaredy!"

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she froze and clung?
qa.a: She was frightened of the big dog.

qa.q: What did Zeenat's mother do that helps her fear?
qa.a: She comforted her, kept a safe distance and let her watch the dog from there instead of mocking or forcing.

qa.q: How might the boy's laughter feel for Zeenat?
qa.a: It might make her feel more upset or ashamed about being scared.

grounding: A bystander sees a mother comfort her fearful toddler and keep a safe distance rather than mock her fear.

passage: Daycare note, first week. Ishita hid behind her father's legs every morning this week and looked away whenever I said hello. I didn't push her to greet me. On Monday and Tuesday she sat on his lap and watched. On Wednesday she took a crayon from the table. On Friday she let go of his hand and sat beside me at the play dough. Sharmila, daycare teacher

qa.q: What did Ishita do on Friday?
qa.a: She let go of her father's hand and sat beside Sharmila at the play dough.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling at the start of the week?
qa.a: She felt shy and unsure with a new teacher and place.

qa.q: What helped Ishita warm up over the week?
qa.a: Sharmila didn't push her to greet, and her father stayed while she watched and came closer at her own pace.

qa.q: How might Ishita's father feel by Friday?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and proud to see her join in.

grounding: A teacher gives a shy toddler warm-up time instead of pushing, and she joins in by the end of the week.

passage:
At the village wedding, Shalini hid behind her mother's sari when all the relatives crowded round. Her aunt Ritu didn't reach for her. She sat on the floor a little way off and rolled a small ball gently toward Shalini's feet.
Shalini looked at it, then at Ritu, then away. Ritu waited. After a long moment, a small foot came out from behind the sari and pushed the ball back.

qa.q: What did Ritu roll toward Shalini?
qa.a: A small ball.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling as she hid behind the sari?
qa.a: She was shy and overwhelmed with so many relatives crowding round.

qa.q: Which of Ritu's choices helped Shalini warm up?
qa.a: Sitting a little way off and rolling a ball without reaching for her, then waiting.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel when the small foot pushes the ball back?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and touched by the small step. 🙂

grounding: An aunt helps a shy toddler warm up with a gentle game instead of pushing her.

passage:
The new neighbour, Rania, came to the door of the Istanbul flat with a plate of pastries. Elif went quiet, looked at the floor and stood behind her mother.
Rania didn't bend down or ask for a hello. She sat and chatted with Elif's mother over tea.
Half an hour later, Elif walked over and put a biscuit on Rania's saucer, without a word.

qa.q: What did Rania bring?
qa.a: A plate of pastries.

qa.q: What was Elif feeling when she looked at the floor?
qa.a: She was shy and unsure with a new person.

qa.q: What did Rania do that helped Elif?
qa.a: She didn't push for a greeting and gave Elif time to warm up.

qa.q: How might Rania feel when Elif offers the biscuit?
qa.a: She would probably feel touched and pleased by the quiet gesture.

grounding: A new neighbour gives a shy toddler warm-up time, and the child approaches in her own way.

passage: Childminder's note, Monday. Nirmala opened every drawer she could reach today, poked her fingers into the plant pot and pointed at everything, asking "Dat?" I named each thing: "spoon", "soil", "clock". We have put a latch on the cleaning cupboard and made one low drawer a "yes drawer" full of safe things to open and pull out. She spent a long time in it. Nandini, childminder

qa.q: What did Nandini put a latch on?
qa.a: The cleaning cupboard.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling as she opened drawers and pointed at everything?
qa.a: She was curious and eager to explore, wanting to know what everything was.

qa.q: Why did Nandini make a "yes drawer"?
qa.a: To keep Nirmala's curiosity safe, giving her things she can explore freely while dangerous things are locked away.

qa.q: How might Nirmala's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel reassured that her curiosity is welcomed and kept safe.

grounding: A childminder names things for a curious toddler and makes the environment safe for exploration.

passage:
In the village yard, Hansa poked a snail on the wall, pulled the lid off the rice tin and pointed up at the sickle hanging from a nail. "Dat?"
"Sickle. Sharp," said Aparna, her grandmother, and moved it higher. "Snail. Slow." She crouched with Hansa to watch it crawl. Hansa leaned in, eyes wide, and touched its shell with one finger.

qa.q: What did Hansa poke on the wall?
qa.a: A snail.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling as she poked, opened and pointed at things?
qa.a: She was curious and eager to learn what everything was.

qa.q: What did Aparna do that kept Hansa's curiosity safe?
qa.a: She moved the sharp sickle higher and named things for her.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel watching Hansa with the snail?
qa.a: She likely feels fond and amused at Hansa's curiosity.

grounding: A grandmother names things for a curious toddler and moves danger out of reach.

passage:
At the park in Stockholm, Sofia stamped in every puddle, turned over stones and squatted to point at a worm. "Dat?"
"A worm," said Freya, her mother. "Wiggly."
Sofia started toward the pond, pointing at the ducks. Freya took her hand. "Ducks! Let's look from here, by the fence." Sofia pressed her face to the fence, pointing and babbling.

qa.q: What did Sofia point at when she squatted?
qa.a: A worm.

qa.q: What was Sofia feeling as she explored the park?
qa.a: She was curious and excited, wanting to know about everything.

qa.q: How did Freya balance curiosity and safety?
qa.a: She named what Sofia found and kept her back from the pond by holding her hand at the fence.

qa.q: What would change if Freya had kept saying no to everything?
qa.a: Sofia's curiosity would be crushed, and she'd learn fewer new words.

grounding: A mother names what her curious toddler finds while keeping her safe near water.

passage:
"Look, Zeenat, the dragon!" Trisha, her big sister, opened the pop-up book. A dragon unfolded off the page.
Zeenat went completely still. She leaned in, mouth open, eyes fixed.
"Now listen!" Trisha pressed all the sound buttons at once. Roars, bells, a trumpet.
Zeenat's eyes slid away to the window. She stared blankly.
"Too much?" said their mother. "Just the dragon, Trisha."

qa.q: What unfolded off the page?
qa.a: A dragon.

qa.q: What did Zeenat's stillness and leaning in show, and what changed?
qa.a: It showed deep interest; when all the sounds went off at once, she stared away because she felt overwhelmed.

qa.q: What did their mother suggest, and why?
qa.a: Just the dragon, because one thing at a time kept Zeenat interested without overwhelming her.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel when her mother says "Too much?"
qa.a: Trisha might feel a bit disappointed, having wanted to show off all the sounds.

grounding: A toddler leans in and goes still with interest at a pop-up book, then looks away when too many sounds overwhelm her.

passage: Daycare note, Tuesday. When the visiting storyteller began, Payal went still, leaned forward and hardly blinked, her mouth a little open. She was fixed on the storyteller's face. When the drums started, she turned and stared out of the window instead, very still in a different way. I moved her a little farther from the drums, and after a while she was watching again. Vinita, daycare teacher

qa.q: What did Payal stare at when the drums started?
qa.a: Out of the window.

qa.q: What did Payal's leaning forward and later staring away suggest?
qa.a: Leaning forward showed interest; staring away when the drums began suggests she felt overwhelmed.

qa.q: Which choice of Vinita's helped Payal, and why?
qa.a: Moving her farther from the drums helped, because it lowered the noise so she could return to watching.

qa.q: How might the storyteller see Payal's attention?

passage:
A cowherd was playing a bamboo flute on the path past the village house. Jatin, on the verandah with Lalremsiami, the neighbour, went still and leaned toward the sound, eyes wide.
Later a wedding band came down the same path, drums and horns blaring. Jatin's face went blank, and he stared away at the wall.
Lalremsiami picked him up and carried him inside, where it was quieter. His body relaxed against her.

qa.q: What instrument was the cowherd playing?
qa.a: A bamboo flute.

qa.q: What did Jatin's blank stare at the wall suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was overwhelmed by the loud band, unlike his earlier interest in the flute.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do that helped Jatin?
qa.a: She took him inside where it was quieter, reducing the noise.

qa.q: What would change if Lalremsiami had held him up to see the band?
qa.a: He would likely have become more overwhelmed and upset.

grounding: A neighbour reads a toddler's leaning in as interest and his staring away as overload, and takes him somewhere quieter.
